name: Rebecca Lemp
social_status: Wife of Stephan Lemp, a respected Nördlingen apothecary; relatively elevated social position for a woman accused in the early phase of the Nördlingen trials; not socially marginal
biography:
Rebecca Lemp was the wife of a Nördlingen apothecary, Stephan Lemp, when she was arrested in the early phase of the Nördlingen witch trials of 1590. She is known to historians primarily through the letters she wrote from prison to her husband — letters preserved in the Nördlingen city archive that Lyndal Roper analyzes extensively in Witch Craze (2004) as among the most significant surviving documents of a witch-trial prisoner's subjective experience.

  Lemp's letters document a woman acutely aware that the confession she would ultimately make was false, extracted by torture, and that her husband and children would be left to understand her as a witch when she was not. In the letters, she protests her innocence directly to Stephan, describes the torture she is undergoing, expresses despair at the impossibility of resisting the interrogators' demands for confession, and begs him not to believe what she will be made to say. The letters are emotionally direct and analytically clear: she understands the mechanism of her own confession's production and documents it for her husband even as it is happening.

  Roper's analysis of the Lemp letters in Witch Craze focuses on them as evidence for the subjective experience of torture-based confession — the intersection of bodily pain, institutional pressure, and the destruction of self that the confessional process produced. Roper argues that the letters reveal how torture did not simply extract false statements but also attacked the accused's sense of identity, and that Lemp's frantic insistence on her own innocence to her husband represents an attempt to preserve a self that the confession was being used to destroy. She was ultimately executed in 1590; the specific date is not preserved in the available scholarly record.
arrest_narrative: Lemp was arrested in the early phase of the Nördlingen trials of 1590, which H.C. Erik Midelfort documents in Witch Hunting in Southwestern Germany (1972) as one of the significant early German urban prosecutions. The mechanism of her specific accusation is not detailed in the available scholarly sources; she may have been named through the cascade naming that characterized the Nördlingen proceedings. Her husband Stephan Lemp, as a respected apothecary, attempted to advocate for her through the channels available to him, including the letters she was able to send from prison — an unusual circumstance suggesting either limited oversight of prisoner communications or deliberate permission.

first_interrogation.method: Interrogation under torture; specific method not documented in available scholarship but consistent with the strappado and related techniques documented for contemporaneous German trials
first_interrogation.initial_response: Protested innocence; wrote letters to husband protesting innocence and describing the impossibility of resisting the interrogators
first_interrogation.duration: Extended imprisonment with multiple torture sessions before confession; specific timeline not preserved

torture_sessions.method: Torture consistent with documented Nördlingen practice; specific method not preserved in available scholarship
torture_sessions.duration: Multiple sessions across the period of imprisonment
torture_sessions.outcome: Produced confession under sustained torture; Lemp documented the coercion in letters to her husband

confession_content.demonic_pact: Confessed under torture to a diabolical compact; Lemp explicitly documented in her letters to her husband that this confession was false and extracted by torture.
confession_content.sabbath_activities: Confessed under torture; content of the confession consistent with the Nördlingen prosecutorial pattern.
confession_content.maleficium_claimed: Confessed under torture to harming community members.
accomplices_named: Accomplices named under torture; specific names not documented in available scholarship.

historiographical_analysis.torture_mechanism: Lemp's case is one of Roper's primary examples in Witch Craze (2004) of the torture-confession dynamic as a subjective psychological process as well as a physical coercive mechanism. Roper analyzes the letters as evidence that the torture process did not merely extract false statements but worked to destroy the accused's sense of selfhood and identity — attacking body and name simultaneously. Ginzburg's framework for understanding how institutional interrogation reshapes testimony to fit expected categories is applicable: the letters document Lemp's awareness that the confession she was being forced to make bore no relationship to her actual experience, and her frantic correspondence represents an attempt to preserve a record of that gap.
historiographical_analysis.plausibility: Lemp's own letters constitute the most direct possible evidence that her confession was false: she wrote explicitly to her husband that she was not a witch, that what she would confess under torture was untrue, and that he should not believe it. Roper treats these letters as primary evidence for the subjective experience of coerced confession. No independent evidence supports any of the charges against her; her elevated social position — as an apothecary's wife — makes the social-marginality explanation inapplicable, consistent with Midelfort's documentation of how German urban trials reached beyond marginal populations.
historiographical_analysis.social_vulnerability: Lemp's case challenges simple social-marginality models: as the wife of a respected apothecary, she was not socially marginal in the sense that characterized many English accused analyzed by Macfarlane and Thomas. Roper's analysis identifies a different vulnerability mechanism in German urban trials: the bodily and psychological vulnerabilities of interrogation under torture, which operated independently of social status. Midelfort's demographic analysis of southwestern German trials documents the pattern in which urban prosecutions, once under way, reached into respectable households as accusations cascaded through the community.

execution_details.method: Execution following conviction; specific method not documented in available scholarship — consistent with German practice of burning following strangulation at the stake
execution_details.final_statement: Not documented in available scholarship; her surviving letters from prison constitute the primary record of her final testimony to her husband.

accusations_against_her: Witchcraft and diabolical compact, as confessed under torture

contemporary_defense.supporters: Her husband Stephan Lemp received her prison letters and presumably attempted to advocate for her; the preservation of the letters in the Nördlingen archive suggests he retained them carefully. The limits of his advocacy are evidenced by her execution.
contemporary_defense.defense_arguments: Her letters to her husband constitute the primary surviving record of her defense: explicit statements of innocence and documentation of the coercive mechanism producing her confession. No formal legal defense survived.

historiographical_significance: Rebecca Lemp's prison letters are among the most significant surviving documents in the historiography of witch-trial subjective experience. Roper's analysis in Witch Craze (2004) uses them as the central evidence for her argument about the psychosexual and psychological dimensions of German witch prosecution — the process by which torture-based interrogation attacked not only bodies but identities. Where Ginzburg's Night Battles (1983) reconstructed subaltern voices through the traces left in inquisitorial records, Lemp's letters provide an unusually direct record of a condemned woman's own understanding of her situation. Midelfort's Witch Hunting in Southwestern Germany (1972) provides the institutional context for the Nördlingen trials within which her case occurred. Her case is also historiographically significant as a documented instance of a non-marginal accused woman — the wife of a professional man — whose social position was insufficient to protect her from a German urban prosecution, complicating social-marginality models derived primarily from English material.
source_method: Nördlingen city archive (letters of Rebecca Lemp to Stephan Lemp, 1590); Roper, Witch Craze (2004), which provides extensive analysis of the letters; Midelfort, Witch Hunting in Southwestern Germany (1972)
scholarly_disagreement: The primary scholarly engagement with Lemp's case is Roper's; Midelfort provides demographic and institutional context. Roper's psychoanalytic interpretive framework for the letters — her emphasis on the psychological destruction wrought by the torture process — is not universally adopted by social historians who prefer structural over psychoanalytic accounts of confession dynamics, but the letters themselves are not contested as primary evidence. The basic facts of Lemp's arrest, correspondence, and execution are not disputed.
primary_document: Letters of Rebecca Lemp to Stephan Lemp (1590), preserved in Nördlingen city archive; analyzed extensively in Roper, Witch Craze (2004)
